summary: Tiny battery-powered devices on IEEE 802.15.4 radio links can form 6LoWPAN networks, but neither the radio standard nor the 6LoWPAN format says how multi-hop mesh routing should work. This informational RFC describes the problem and sets out routing requirements that take account of low power and other limits of such devices.

eli5.summary: Little sensors with weak batteries need to pass messages along to each other, like kids passing notes across a classroom. This memo lists what a good note-passing system must handle.

questions: what are the routing requirements for 6lowpan
what is the difference between route-over and mesh-under
why is ipsec hard on 6lowpan devices
subtitle: What a routing protocol for tiny, battery-powered 802.15.4 devices has to cope with, written down before anyone designs one.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.15.4 networks can form meshes, but neither that standard nor the 6LoWPAN format specification says how a mesh is built and maintained, and existing IP routing protocols may not fit devices with a few KB of RAM and a battery.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the design space (route-over versus mesh-under), lists the scenario and link parameters that matter, and then states routing requirements R01 to R18 for devices, links, network behaviour, security, mesh-under forwarding and management.
tldr.outcome: It recommends no solution. It is layer-agnostic input for groups such as the IETF ROLL working group that design routing protocols relevant to 6LoWPANs.

today: RFC 6606 is an Informational RFC (May 2012) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It gives requirements rather than a protocol, and it names the IETF ROLL working group as one intended consumer of its guidance.

sections.title: The Problem with Routing on Tiny Devices
sections.content:
A 6LoWPAN is a network of devices that follow the IEEE 802.15.4 standard and carry IPv6 as described in RFC 4944. Such devices have low bandwidth, short range, little memory and weak processors. The RFC gives typical figures of a few KB of RAM, a few dozen KB of ROM or flash, and a few MHz of CPU, running on a primary battery.

IEEE 802.15.4 supports star and mesh topologies, but neither it nor RFC 4944 defines how a mesh is obtained and maintained. Existing IP routing protocols may not fit, because nodes have special roles, sleep most of the time, and must save power.

The 6LoWPAN problem statement (RFC 4919) already named four basic needs: low overhead on data packets, low routing overhead, minimal memory and computation, and support for sleeping nodes. This RFC expands them into detailed requirements. It focuses on stub networks, and it does not imply that one routing solution suits every application.
sections.eli5: Tiny gadgets run on a small battery and have very little memory, so they cannot use the same heavy mail-sorting rules that big computers use. This memo explains why and says what is needed.

sections.title: Route-Over and Mesh-Under
sections.content:
The RFC separates two places where multi-hop forwarding can happen. With route-over, routing is done at the IP layer. All routers (6LoWPAN Border Routers, or 6LBRs, and 6LoWPAN Routers, or 6LRs) perform IP routing inside the stub network, and the link-local scope covers the nodes within symmetric radio range of a node.

With mesh-under, forwarding happens below the IP link, in the adaptation layer. The whole 6LoWPAN looks like a single IP link, the 6LBR is the only IPv6 router, and 64-bit (or 16-bit short) link-layer addresses are used rather than IP addresses. A mesh-under mechanism MUST be provided to support multi-hop transmission in that case.

In both cases addresses are not assigned by topology. They typically come from EUI-64 addresses fixed at manufacturing time or from a roughly random assignment of 16-bit MAC addresses, so there is no aggregation beyond sharing common prefixes. The RFC also says routing packets should fit into a single IEEE 802.15.4 frame.
sections.eli5: Passing a note can be done by the postal system (route-over) or by kids in the classroom handing it along without the teacher noticing (mesh-under). Both get the note across, but they work at different levels.

sections.title: Scenario and Link Parameters
sections.content:
Because applications vary so much, the RFC lists parameters that describe a scenario in which a routing protocol could be evaluated. Network properties include number of devices, density and diameter, connectivity (from always connected to rarely connected), mobility, deployment, spatial distribution, traffic patterns, classes of service and security. Node parameters include processing speed, memory, power source, transmission range and traffic load.

For random placement, the RFC quotes that an average of 7 neighbors per node gives approximately 95% network connectivity, and 10 neighbors give 99%.

Link parameters cover throughput and latency for legacy IEEE 802.15.4 in ideal conditions. At 2.4 GHz, throughput with 16-bit MAC addresses in unreliable mode is 151.6 kbit/s; at 868 MHz it is 15.5 kbit/s. The RFC warns that multi-criteria routing metrics may be too expensive for 6LoWPAN nodes.
sections.eli5: Before judging a note-passing plan you need to know how many kids there are, how far they sit apart, how tired they get and how fast each can pass. This part lists those questions.

sections.title: Requirements for Devices, Links and Networks
sections.content:
Requirements R01 to R13 come in three groups. For device properties, protocols SHOULD allow small code size and low routing state (R01), noting that a routing table may be limited to fewer than 32 entries and that there should be at least one mode that works with 32 forwarding entries or less. They SHOULD also minimize power use through efficient control packets (R02).

For link properties, control messages SHOULD NOT exceed a single IEEE 802.15.4 frame (R03), since the standard specifies an MTU of 127 bytes, about 80 octets of MAC payload with security enabled. Protocols must consider delivery probability (R04) and latency needs (R05), SHOULD be robust to link failure (R06) and SHOULD operate correctly with link asymmetry (R07).

For network characteristics, protocols SHOULD account for nodes that hibernate (R08), use a flexible metric that can combine inputs such as LQI and energy balance (R09), scale from a few nodes to maybe millions (R10), keep route repair cheap (R11), allow dynamic topologies and mobile nodes (R12) and support point-to-point, point-to-multipoint and multipoint-to-point traffic (R13). R09 MUST consider mains-powered nodes as relay points.

The RFC's worked example (Figure 4) shows why hop count alone can mislead: a one-hop path with delivery ratio 0.6 needs 1.67 average transmissions, while a two-hop path with 0.9 per link needs 2.22 but delivers 0.81.
sections.eli5: The note-passers must not waste energy, must keep notes small, must cope when a friend falls asleep or moves, and must still get most notes through on time. Those are the rules in this part.

sections.title: Security Requirement
sections.content:
R14 says 6LoWPAN routing protocols MUST support confidentiality, authentication and integrity services for the secure delivery of control messages. The RFC explains that attackers can feed false routing information, replay captured packets or drain batteries by sending broadcast messages or redirecting routes.

Security is costly here. Public key primitives are typically avoided as too expensive, and the RFC doubts that IPsec fits as is: it needs an extra header (AH or ESP) in every packet, and key management with IKEv2 adds signaling. A 6LoWPAN may therefore need its own keying method with minimal overhead.

The IEEE 802.15.4 MAC provides an AES-based security mechanism, which in the worst case consumes 21 bytes of MAC payload. Because IEEE 802.15.4 does not protect acknowledgment frames, an adversary can forge them, so in high-security applications the routing protocol must not rely on acknowledgment feedback. Section 6 repeats that a static security configuration does not suffice in dynamic ad hoc 6LoWPANs.
sections.eli5: Someone could slip fake notes into the chain or wear out everyone's batteries. The system needs a lock on its messages, but the lock has to be light enough for a tiny gadget to carry.

sections.title: Mesh-Under Forwarding and Management
sections.content:
Requirements R15 to R17 apply to mesh-under forwarding and are aimed at bodies that might work on routing below IP, such as the IEEE. A mesh-under protocol MUST support both 16-bit short and 64-bit extended MAC addresses (R15). Nodes SHOULD avoid sending separate Hello messages and MAY use link-layer mechanisms such as acknowledgments to track active neighbors (R16). If IP multicast is enabled, the protocol MAY use network structure to limit link-layer broadcast (R17).

R18 says a routing protocol SHOULD follow the operations and management guidelines of RFC 5706. The RFC favors automatic configuration of parameters, since a 6LoWPAN can have a large number of devices without user interfaces, and monitoring of routing table entries and fault logs.
sections.eli5: Kids who pass notes by hand should not keep shouting hello to check on neighbors, and the whole setup should arrange itself so nobody has to fiddle with every gadget.
